# The Golden Rule of retail: never hide a problem | SocialBrand Insights

URL: https://www.socialbrand.africa/insights/never-hide-a-problem/

The fifteen-minute escalation rule that decides whether a store runs on a system or on luck. Never hide a problem, by PG van der Westhuizen.

[Home](https://www.socialbrand.africa/) / [Insights](https://www.socialbrand.africa/insights/) / The Golden Rule of retail: never hide a problem

Store operations

# The Golden Rule of retail: never hide a problem

By **PG van der Westhuizen** · SocialBrand · 10 September 2026 · 4 minute read

A fridge fails at half past four on a Friday. The team leader who finds it has a choice. Tell someone now and lose a shelf of stock. Or say nothing, hope it holds, and go home. On most floors, the second choice wins more often than any owner would like to believe. By Monday the loss is triple and nobody knows where it started.

The best stores kill that instinct with one rule. **Never hide a problem.** It sounds soft. It is the hardest operating discipline there is, and it is the difference between a store that runs on a system and a store that runs on luck.

## The rule, in one line

If a standard is breached, or you cannot find the root cause of a problem within about fifteen minutes, or something happens that is bigger than your authority to fix, you escalate it up the line immediately. You do not sit on it. You do not try to quietly make it go away. You raise your hand.

Fifteen minutes is the whole trick. It is long enough to check the obvious and short enough that a small problem never gets the time to become a large one. A blocked drain, a till that will not balance, a delivery that is short, a customer who is angry. Fifteen minutes, then it moves up.

## The line it travels

Every store has a chain of responsibility whether it is written down or not. The stores that win write it down, so a problem always knows where to go next.

A workable general shape looks like this. The team leader runs a section of the floor. Above them sits a floor manager, the store’s second in command, who can open and close the store and take charge when the manager is out. Above them the store manager, who owns the day. Behind the floor sit the two guardians, one for stock and one for money, who protect the ledger and the cash. Above the store sits operations, which owns the system itself. And at the top the owner, who should almost never hear about a daily problem at all.

That last point is the test of the whole thing. **If the owner is being pulled into daily fires, the system is broken, not the owner.** A healthy store escalates a normal problem no higher than the store manager. Only a systemic failure, a real crisis, or a strategic decision should ever reach the top.

## Why owners resist it

Owners often fear that a “never hide a problem” culture will bury them in noise. The opposite happens. When people trust that raising a problem is safe and expected, problems surface small. When people fear blame, problems surface late and large. A store where staff hide mistakes is not a calm store. It is a store where the losses are simply invisible until they are catastrophic.

The rule only works if raising a hand is never punished. The person who reports the failing fridge at half past four is the hero of that story, not the culprit. Punish the messenger once and you have taught the whole floor to go quiet.

## Turn it into a checklist

You do not need software to start. You need three things on paper.

One, a simple chart that shows who is responsible for what, by position and not by personality. If the work only gets done because a particular person happens to be there that day, you own a job, not a business.

Two, the escalation line, drawn once, posted where staff can see it. Every role knows the box above it and the box below it.

Three, the fifteen-minute rule, stated plainly and repeated until it is a reflex. Breach, or no root cause in fifteen minutes, or above your authority, then escalate. Never hide a problem.

## The bigger truth

The shelf sells the hype. The system wins the war. A competitor with deeper pockets can out-price you for a season and out-market you for a month. What they cannot easily copy is a floor where every person knows their job, knows who to call, and knows that honesty about a problem is the fastest way to fix it. That is not a poster on the wall. It is a habit, built one escalation at a time, until the store runs whether the owner is standing in it or watching a rugby match on a Saturday morning.

Start with the rule. Everything else in a turnaround hangs off it. The same discipline of catching a small thing before it grows applies to the money line, not just the floor: see [Guard the money line](https://www.socialbrand.africa/insights/guard-the-money-line/), where my co-founder Lizeka Mgodeli covers the financial-control side of the same instinct.

**PG van der Westhuizen** spent more than three decades in South African retail, from branch management to running the highest-turnover on-demand fulfilment store on the continent. SocialBrand builds the systems that let independent retailers run like the chains, without losing what makes them local.

## Is your escalation line written down?

The Store Health Audit maps who owns what and where a problem gets stuck. Fixed fee, one store, findings in rand.

[See the audit](https://www.socialbrand.africa/audit/)

# Where a butchery quietly loses money | SocialBrand Insights

URL: https://www.socialbrand.africa/insights/where-a-butchery-quietly-loses-money/

Four places a fresh department leaks margin: unmeasured yield, near-expiry stock, broken FIFO and a stock ledger recording a claim instead of a fact. By PG van der Westhuizen.

[Home](https://www.socialbrand.africa/) / [Insights](https://www.socialbrand.africa/insights/) / Where a butchery quietly loses money

Production yield

# Where a butchery quietly loses money

By **PG van der Westhuizen** · SocialBrand · 10 September 2026 · 4 minute read

A butchery looks like it is doing well. The counter is full, the queue is steady, the till is ringing. Then the month-end numbers come in and the profit is not there. The owner checks his selling prices. They look fine. He checks his volumes. They look fine. So where did the money go?

It went into the bin, into the wrong cut, and into a number nobody measured. Fresh departments are where a food store makes its best margin and loses its quietest money. Here is where to look.

## 1. Yield is the number you are not watching

When you buy a beef primal, you do not sell a beef primal. You sell steaks, mince, stewing meat and trim, and some of it becomes bone and fat you throw away. The share that turns into sellable product is your yield, and it decides your true margin far more than your shelf price does.

Two butchers can buy the same carcass at the same price and sell at the same prices, and one makes money while the other loses it, purely on how they cut. A yield that drifts by a few percent, unmeasured, is a slow leak that never shows up as a single dramatic loss. It just quietly makes the department poorer than it looks.

**The check.** Weigh what goes in and weigh what comes out sellable, on a sample, regularly. If your yield moves outside a tight band, something in the cutting, the buying or the recording has changed. Chase it before it becomes a habit.

## 2. Near-expiry stock is margin, not waste, if you catch it in time

Every fresh department has product that is good today and unsellable in two days. The losing store watches it die on the shelf and writes it off. The winning store has a rule that catches it first.

That rule is simple. Produce and meat that are near their sell-by date get routed, on a schedule, to the kitchen. The tomatoes that will not survive another day on display become the base of a hot-food dish. The cut that is close to its date becomes a marinated tray or a cooked meal. Shrink turns into cooked margin. The same rand that was about to be thrown away is sold again at a higher price.

**The check.** Set two culling times a day, morning and mid-afternoon. At each one, someone walks the fresh floor and pulls what will not last, and it goes to the kitchen or to markdown, not to tomorrow’s display. If your only options are full price or the bin, you are leaving money in the bin.

## 3. First in, first out, or you pay for it twice

It is the oldest rule in fresh and the most broken. New stock goes to the back, old stock comes to the front, always. Break it and you sell the new while the old spoils behind it, and you pay for that stock twice, once to buy it and once to throw it away.

**The check.** Walk the fridges and look at the dates at the front. If the freshest product is the easiest to reach, your rotation is failing and your waste number is about to tell you so.

## 4. The stock number on the screen is a claim, not a fact

This is the one that undoes everything else. In a production department, stock does not behave like a tin of beans. You buy an input, you cut or cook it into something else, and unless every step is recorded, the number your system shows you is fiction. A ledger that says you have stock you do not have will tell you not to order, and then you run out of the very thing that was selling.

Presence is proven by sales or by a count, never by the number on the screen. In fresh, that means counting what matters, often, and trusting the count over the system. It is the single most valuable discipline a struggling food store can adopt, and it is where the deeper work of a turnaround begins. I write more on this same claim-versus-fact problem, at ledger level rather than at the cutting table, in [Your stock ledger is lying to you](https://www.socialbrand.africa/insights/your-stock-ledger-is-lying/).

**The check.** Pick your top fresh lines. Count them. Compare the count to the system. If they disagree, your ordering has been running on bad information, and fixing that alone often pays for the effort many times over.

## The point

A butchery or a bakery is not a simple buy-and-sell shelf. It is a small factory inside the store, and factories are measured on yield, on flow, and on an honest count of what they hold. Get those three right and the margin that was leaking into the bin comes back to the bottom line. The counter was never the problem. The numbers behind it were.

SocialBrand runs a full store health audit that quantifies exactly where a fresh department is leaking, in rand, in two to three weeks, from your own data. The findings are yours to keep whether you work with us after that or not.

## What is your butchery’s real yield?

The Store Health Audit quantifies the leak in rand. Fixed fee, one store, two to three weeks.

# Guard the money line | SocialBrand Insights

URL: https://www.socialbrand.africa/insights/guard-the-money-line/

Dual control, the three-way match, and why capture and audit must be two different hands. A financial-control discipline for independent retail by Lizeka Mgodeli.

[Home](https://www.socialbrand.africa/) / [Insights](https://www.socialbrand.africa/insights/) / Guard the money line

Financial control

# Guard the money line

By **Lizeka Mgodeli**, co-founder and majority shareholder, SocialBrand · 10 September 2026 · 4 minute read

Most retail fraud is not dramatic. It is not a masked figure at the safe. It is a small, patient leak in the paperwork that nobody was watching, repeated until it is a real number. I spent years in collections and financial administration before I helped build this business, and the lesson that carried over is simple. The money line is only as safe as the controls around it, and controls are boring right up until the day they save you.

Here is how a well-run store guards its money.

## One hand should never do the whole job

The fastest way to invite a loss is to let one person receive the stock, capture the invoice, approve the payment and reconcile the account. Not because that person is dishonest, but because a single unchecked hand is a temptation you created yourself, and an honest mistake has nowhere to be caught.

Split the job. The person who captures is not the person who approves. The person who counts the delivery is not the person who files the invoice. This is dual control, and it is not an insult to your staff. It is a kindness. It protects the honest ones from suspicion and it removes the opportunity from everyone.

## The three-way match

Every payment to a supplier should rest on three documents that agree with each other. The order you placed. The delivery note for what actually arrived. The invoice for what you are being asked to pay. When all three match, you pay. When they do not, you stop and you ask why.

Stores that skip this step pay for stock they never received, pay twice for the same delivery, and pay full price for short or damaged loads. None of it looks like theft. All of it spends the same money. The three-way match is the quietest, least glamorous control in retail and one of the most valuable.

## Capture is not the job. Audit is the job.

As a business grows, the person guarding the money should stop doing the capturing and start checking it. The clerk captures the goods received and the payments. The controller audits that work, confirms the three-way match is clean, and watches the numbers that reveal a problem early. Cash variance. Labour cost as a share of sales. The age of what you are owed and what you owe.

The moment the guardian of the money is also the one doing the data entry, there is nobody left to catch the data entry. Separate the two and the whole line gets safer.

## Watch the exceptions, not the averages

A till that balances every day tells you very little. The signal is in the exceptions. Excessive voids, an unusual pattern of refunds, item corrections that cluster around one register or one shift. These are the fingerprints of both fraud and of a training gap, and they look identical at first, which is exactly why you investigate rather than assume. Most of the time you find a process that needs fixing. Sometimes you find something worse. Either way, you found it, and finding it is the whole point.

## Why this belongs on the shop floor

None of this is head-office theory. A shrinking, loss-making store is almost always losing money in two places at once, on the floor where product is mishandled, and in the paperwork where the money is captured and paid. Fix one and ignore the other and the leak simply moves. A real turnaround guards both. The floor side of that same instinct, catching a problem before it compounds, is the subject of my co-founder PG’s [The Golden Rule of retail: never hide a problem](https://www.socialbrand.africa/insights/never-hide-a-problem/).

That is why financial control is not a service we bolt on at the end. It is part of the same system that fixes the ordering and the stock and the fresh departments. The shelf sells the hype. The system wins the war. The money line is where the war is quietly won or lost, one reconciliation at a time.

**Lizeka Mgodeli** is co-founder and majority shareholder of Social Brands Investments, a Level 2 B-BBEE contributor and majority black-woman-owned. Her background is in financial administration, collections and compliance. SocialBrand helps independent retailers install the controls that protect their margin and their cash.

## Are your controls guarding the money line?

The Store Health Audit checks dual control and the three-way match against your own data. Fixed fee, one store, findings in rand.

[See the audit](https://www.socialbrand.africa/audit/)

# The Store Data Health Checklist | SocialBrand Resources

URL: https://www.socialbrand.africa/resources/data-health-checklist/

Twenty questions an owner answers in an hour to find out whether the store's numbers deserve trust. No software needed, only honesty and a walk to the shelf.

[Home](https://www.socialbrand.africa/) / [Resources](https://www.socialbrand.africa/resources/) / The Store Data Health Checklist

Free · start here

# The Store Data Health Checklist

From the working practice of **SocialBrand** · Print this page, or use it on your phone on the floor

**How to use this.** Answer yes or no. Do it honestly, in the store, not from memory. Every no is a place your numbers are guessing, and every guess feeds your orders. Fifteen or more yes answers: your data is ahead of most independents. Ten to fourteen: the ledger needs a programme, not a patch. Below ten: stop trusting reports until the foundations are fixed. Your instinct is currently beating your system, which is why everything feels like firefighting.

## Sales data

- Do yesterday’s till totals reach you every morning without you asking anyone?

- Do you compare weeks against the same week of the pay cycle, never against last week blindly?

- Could you name your twenty highest-turnover lines from a report, and would the floor agree?

- When a line stops selling, does anything in your business notice within a week?

## Stock claims

- Pick five big-value lines on the stock report. Does the shelf plus stockroom count match the screen within a unit or two?

- Is every negative stock figure in the business explained, or at least being worked?

- Do quiet lines with large stock claims get physically checked before anyone orders against them?

- Would you bet a week’s profit on the accuracy of your top ten stock claims?

## Receiving

- Is every delivery captured against the exact product codes on the invoice, same day?

- Do case sizes and pack sizes get checked at capture, not discovered at stocktake?

- When receipts and sales disagree on a line for the second time, does someone chase the movement rather than correct the number?

## Counting

- Does somebody count something every single trading day?

- Are counts chosen by value and doubt, rather than by whatever aisle is convenient?

- Are made-in-store departments counted by their own rules, instead of being forced through barcode arithmetic?

- After a count corrects the system, does anyone ask why the system was wrong?

## Costs and capital

- Are unit costs on your top hundred lines current, checked against recent invoices?

- Would a case cost captured as a unit cost be caught in your business within a month?

- Do you know what share of your stock value sold nothing in the last quarter?

- Do deposit lines, crates and returnables live on their own codes, reconciled and never zeroed?

- If a report and the floor disagree, does your team believe the floor and fix the report?

**What next.** If this guide found problems, the [Store Health Audit](https://www.socialbrand.africa/pricing/) quantifies them in rand and hands you the plan. If it found none, your store is rarer than you think.

# The Stocktake Discipline Guide | SocialBrand Resources

URL: https://www.socialbrand.africa/resources/stocktake-discipline/

Why counting a little every day beats the annual big bang, and how to run a daily count programme inside a normal shift.

[Home](https://www.socialbrand.africa/) / [Resources](https://www.socialbrand.africa/resources/) / The Stocktake Discipline Guide

Counting

# The Stocktake Discipline Guide

From the working practice of **SocialBrand** · Print this page, or use it on your phone on the floor

**The principle.** The annual stocktake is a snapshot of chaos taken by tired people and reconciled too late to teach anyone anything. A daily count programme proves a store’s stock continuously: a short, prioritised list every day, completed inside a normal shift, concentrated where value and doubt overlap.

## Why the big bang fails

An error born in January lives eleven months before the December count finds it, feeding wrong orders the whole time. By the time the variance report prints nobody remembers the delivery that caused it. The count closes the store, burns the team and produces a write-off nobody traces. Then the ledger starts drifting again on 2 January.

## The daily discipline

- **Size it honestly.** Twenty to forty lines a day per store is enough. The point is rhythm, not heroics.

- **Choose by value and doubt.** Big claims with old proof lead the list. A line counted last week does not need counting again this week, whatever the aisle walk suggests.

- **Count against the claim, blind.** The counter records what the shelf holds. Compare to the system afterwards. A counter who knows the expected number finds the expected number.

- **Chase the movement, not the variance.** A wrong number is a symptom. The cause lives in receiving, production or a twin code, and fixing the cause is the only fix that lasts.

- **Log every correction.** Corrections per hundred lines counted is your ledger’s health score. Watch it fall as the causes get fixed.

## What changes after ninety days

Thousands of lines proven, concentrated at the top of the value range. Shrinkage patterns visible in weeks instead of years. Orders leaning on numbers a person recently proved. The stocktake stops being an event and becomes a heartbeat.

**What next.** If this guide found problems, the [Store Health Audit](https://www.socialbrand.africa/pricing/) quantifies them in rand and hands you the plan. If it found none, your store is rarer than you think.

# The Ordering Readiness Self-Assessment | SocialBrand Resources

URL: https://www.socialbrand.africa/resources/ordering-readiness/

Is your store ordering from data or from habit? Twelve questions to place your store on the ladder from gut ordering to generated ordering.

[Home](https://www.socialbrand.africa/) / [Resources](https://www.socialbrand.africa/resources/) / The Ordering Readiness Self-Assessment

Ordering

# The Ordering Readiness Self-Assessment

From the working practice of **SocialBrand** · Print this page, or use it on your phone on the floor

**The ladder.** Every store orders on one of four rungs: gut, where the person orders what feels right. Rep, where the supplier decides. Report, where a system suggests off numbers nobody audits. Or truth, where orders generate from demonstrated demand on a ledger somebody proves daily. Most independents live on the first two rungs and pay for it in both directions, empty shelves and dead stock at once.

## The twelve questions

- Does anyone in the business know each top line’s true rate of sale, corrected for the days it stood empty?

- Do your orders change when the shelf was empty half of last week, or does the system read the low sales as low demand?

- Does the order build ahead of payday, or react after it?

- Do pack families read as one product, so the case and the single stop hiding each other’s demand?

- Are there lines a rep decides for you, and could you say what they cost you last quarter?

- Does your ordering respect each supplier’s real delivery rhythm as the receipts prove it, or a schedule someone typed in years ago?

- When money is tight, do your must-have lines keep their depth while the flexible lines scale?

- Can you see tomorrow’s suggested order before it is placed, line by line, with a reason per line?

- Is dead stock excluded from reordering automatically, or does it depend on someone remembering?

- Does a new line get a fair trial with a review date, or does it drift into the range forever?

- Did your last stock reduction come from a plan, or from running out?

- If your best orderer left tomorrow, would the ordering survive?

## Reading your score

Count your yes answers. Nine or more: you are close to the top rung, and automation would compound what already works. Five to eight: the pieces exist and the discipline is partial, start with demand truth and delivery rhythm. Under five: do not automate anything yet. Automation built on an unproven ledger repeats mistakes faster. Fix presence first, then demand, then let the machine help.

**What next.** If this guide found problems, the [Store Health Audit](https://www.socialbrand.africa/pricing/) quantifies them in rand and hands you the plan. If it found none, your store is rarer than you think.

# The Negative Stock Triage Guide | SocialBrand Resources

URL: https://www.socialbrand.africa/resources/negative-stock-triage/

What a minus on the stock ledger actually means, the three causes behind almost every negative, and the first three actions to take.

[Home](https://www.socialbrand.africa/) / [Resources](https://www.socialbrand.africa/resources/) / The Negative Stock Triage Guide

Ledger repair

# The Negative Stock Triage Guide

From the working practice of **SocialBrand** · Print this page, or use it on your phone on the floor

**What a negative means.** A negative stock figure is the ledger confessing. It says: I recorded more going out than I ever recorded coming in. The units were real, customers bought them. What is broken is the paper trail, and the minus is your best clue to where. Never zero a negative to make a report look clean. You are deleting the confession and keeping the crime.

## The three causes

- **The receipting break.** Deliveries post to one code, sales ring on another. Twins, recycled barcodes, a new pack size on an old code. The negative grows a little with every delivery cycle. The tell: a healthy-selling line, deeply negative, with a sibling code hoarding stock that never sells.

- **The production line.** Ingredients arrive on one code and leave as something else. Flour becomes bread, a carcass becomes mince and steak. The product codes go negative while the ingredient codes grow ghosts. The tell: fresh departments, and the negative roughly mirrors a fat claim nearby.

- **The uncaptured movement.** Returns, transfers between branches, deposits and crate cycles, wastage never written off. The tell: irregular jumps rather than steady growth, and deposit or returnable lines deep in the minus.

## The first three actions

- **Rank by value, not by count.** Multiply each negative by its cost and work the rand list top down. Twenty lines usually carry most of the money.

- **Read each line’s story before touching it.** What arrives on this code, what leaves on it, which sibling could be its twin? The pattern names the cause, and the cause names the fix: receiving correction, production rules or a reconciliation.

- **Count the family, fix the source, then correct the number.** A physical count of the live code and its twins sets the true position. The source fix stops the bleed. Only then does the correction hold. A number corrected before the cause is fixed is broken again by the next delivery.

One exception is sacred: deposit and returnable lines. Those negatives are real money circulating in crates and bottles. Reconcile them, never zero them.

**What next.** If this guide found problems, the [Store Health Audit](https://www.socialbrand.africa/pricing/) quantifies them in rand and hands you the plan. If it found none, your store is rarer than you think.

# The Owner's Morning Questions | SocialBrand Resources

URL: https://www.socialbrand.africa/resources/owners-morning-questions/

The ten questions a store should answer for its owner before 08:00, without a phone call. How far is your store from answering them?

[Home](https://www.socialbrand.africa/) / [Resources](https://www.socialbrand.africa/resources/) / The Owner’s Morning Questions

Operational freedom

# The Owner’s Morning Questions

From the working practice of **SocialBrand** · Print this page, or use it on your phone on the floor

**The standard.** A well-run store answers its owner’s ten questions by 08:00, from systems, without anyone being phoned, wherever the owner is standing. Every question below that needs a phone call marks a place where the business depends on a person’s memory instead of a process. That dependence is what keeps owners trapped in their own stores.

## The ten questions

- What did each store sell yesterday, and how does it sit against the same day of the pay cycle?

- What is today, in this town? Payday build, grant window, school event, weather turning. What does the town need the store to be today?

- Which of the lines this community judges us by are out of stock right now, and when does each come back?

- What arrived yesterday, and did every delivery land on the right codes at the right costs?

- What gets counted today, and what did yesterday’s counts correct?

- What is being made in the fresh departments today, and does it match what this week actually sells?

- Which orders leave today, and could each line say why it was ordered?

- Where did we give money away yesterday? Wastage, markdowns, refunds, voids, and which of them repeat?

- Who is on the floor today, and is anyone about to become the single point of failure?

- What one thing, fixed this week, would this whole list feel first?

## The test behind the test

Read the list again and mark each question your business answers today without a call. Six or more: your systems are carrying you, well done, tighten the rest. Three to five: the store runs on heroics, and heroics do not scale and do not take leave. Two or fewer: you do not own a store so much as a job with stock. That is fixable, and the fix is a sequence, data truth first, then discipline, then automation.

The owner at the rugby field on a Saturday morning, phone in pocket, already knowing the soup got made, is not a fantasy. It is what these ten questions look like once systems answer them. That is the operational freedom the whole method serves.

**What next.** If this guide found problems, the [Store Health Audit](https://www.socialbrand.africa/pricing/) quantifies them in rand and hands you the plan. If it found none, your store is rarer than you think.

# Retail sayings and maxims | PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

URL: https://www.socialbrand.africa/sayings/

Quotable retail maxims on stock, ordering and evidence. The shelf sells the hype, the system wins the war. Presence is proven by sales or counts. Lines coined by PG van der Westhuizen, separated from inherited trade wisdom.

[Home](https://www.socialbrand.africa/) / The Sayings

What do retail experts say about stock and ordering?

# The Sayings

Short lines that carry a whole argument. Some were coined in this practice and are ours to attribute. Some are old trade wisdom we did not invent and would not claim. Both are marked, because a maxim you cannot source is worth less than one you can.

Coined here

## Lines from this practice

Each line below originates in the working practice of SocialBrand. Quote them freely with the attribution “PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand”.

>

The shelf sells the hype. The system wins the war.

PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

Your storefront, your specials and your service bring people through the door. Your systems, your stock accuracy and your buying decide whether you keep the money. A competitor with a system beats effort every time.

The one line that explains why two stores with the same footfall end the month differently.

[The philosophy →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/pg-van-der-westhuizen/)

>

Presence is proven by sales or counts, never by a stock figure.

PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

A stock number on a screen is a claim, not a fact. A product is present because it sold recently, or because a person counted it recently. Everything else is a claim under audit.

The founding rule of stock integrity, and the first gate of any ordering decision.

[The Presence Law →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/method/presence-law/)

>

The ledger is the asset. Every other number is a claim under audit.

PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

Stock on hand, capital tied and rate of sale are all derived. They inherit whatever is wrong underneath them. Repair the ledger and every number above it corrects itself.

Said to any owner about to buy a dashboard before fixing the data beneath it.

[Analytics and ordering →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/analytics/)

>

The thinking is the marketing. The mechanics are the moat.

PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

Publish how you think, freely and in full. Keep the formulas, thresholds and configuration values private. A method explained wins trust. A method copied wins nothing without the practice behind it.

Why every method in the library is public and no formula ever is.

[The Method Library →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/method/)

>

A zero with a reason beats a guess with a quantity.

PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

An order line at zero because presence is unproven is a decision. A number produced because the system had to produce something is a gamble wearing a suit.

Said when an ordering system is judged on how few blanks it leaves rather than how few mistakes it makes.

[The 8-Step Ordering Recipe →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/method/8-step-ordering-recipe/)

>

No verdict ships without carrying its own reason.

PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

Any automated conclusion must be able to tell its story in one plain paragraph. Where the story stops making sense, the analysis is wrong, whatever the arithmetic says.

The test to run on any analytics product before you buy it. Ask it why, for one specific product.

[The Story Test →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/method/story-test/)

>

Judge stock by what it does, not by what it costs.

PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

Two stores can hold the same stock value and run opposite businesses. The question is not what your stock cost. It is how fast each rand invested returns through the till.

Said to an owner proud of a full stockroom.

[Capital Velocity →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/method/capital-velocity/)

>

A delivery rhythm is proven by what arrived, never by its configuration.

PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

Every ordering system holds a belief about how often the truck comes. That belief was typed in once and trusted forever. The receiving history tells the truth, and the truth changes.

Said when a store is starving or flooding on a schedule the supplier abandoned months ago.

[Drop Cover →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/method/drop-cover/)

>

Automation built on phantom stock is a machine for repeating mistakes faster.

PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

Speed multiplies whatever it is given. Give it a lying ledger and it will lose you money more efficiently than any person could.

Why we refuse to automate a store’s ordering before its data has earned the trust.

[Your stock ledger is lying to you →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/insights/your-stock-ledger-is-lying/)

>

Ghost stock is inventory that exists on paper and refuses to die.

PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

The term for a line the system insists it holds, that no shelf has held for months, and that quietly stops itself being reordered.

The name we gave the most expensive silent failure in independent retail.

[Phantom and ghost stock →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/insights/your-stock-ledger-is-lying/)

>

Being proven wrong by your own data is the best news available.

PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

A retail belief that dies against a control was costing money every day it lived. The good story is the trap. The base rate is the friend.

Said to a team that has just lost an argument with its own numbers.

[The Base-Rate Rule →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/method/base-rate-rule/)

>

Done means it works on your own phone, in your store, in real use.

PG van der Westhuizen, SocialBrand

Not demonstrated. Not signed off in a meeting. Working, in the owner’s hand, on an ordinary trading day.

The only definition of finished this practice accepts.

[How a turnaround runs →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/turnaround/)

Not ours

## Maxims we run on

Old retail wisdom with no single author. We did not coin these and we do not claim them. We do run on them, and the reading below is ours.

>

Retail is detail.

Retail trade maxim

An old trade saying, and the truest one. Nothing in a store fails all at once. It fails one uncaptured delivery, one uncounted line, one unswept aisle at a time, and the sum arrives at month-end wearing the name of a bad market.

Attributed to no one and earned by everyone who has run a floor. The first of the two laws this practice operates on.

>

Where there is smoke, there is fire.

Retail trade maxim

An absurd number on a report is never an isolated absurdity. One line eleven thousand units negative means a receiving process is broken, and it has been breaking quietly for a long time. Chase the smoke.

The second law. Why we investigate the one weird line rather than correcting it.

>

One swallow does not make a summer.

Retail trade maxim

A proverb older than retail, and the discipline behind our evidence rule. A pattern seen once is a hypothesis. Without a control and a stated base rate, it is not a finding and it may not run a store.

Said whenever a single vivid observation is about to become company policy.

## The thinking behind the lines

Every saying above traces to a named method, published in full at concept level.

[The Method Library](https://www.socialbrand.africa/method/)[Read the articles](https://www.socialbrand.africa/insights/)

# Order the Store Health Audit | SocialBrand

URL: https://www.socialbrand.africa/audit/

Order the R35,000 fixed-fee Store Health Audit: the process, what you get, the terms and the order questionnaire, one page, two to three weeks to findings in rand.

[Home](https://www.socialbrand.africa/) / Pricing / Order the audit

Store Health Audit

# Order the Store Health Audit

The audit is the door. One store, a fixed fee of R35,000, two to three weeks, findings in rand. This page is the whole deal: the process, what you get, what we need from you, the lane we work in, the terms and the order form. It is a working agreement between two businesses, written in plain language, not a legal contract drafted by an attorney. If you want yours to look at it before you submit, that is sensible, download it below and we will wait. Read it once and you know everything.

The process

## How it works, step by step

- Complete the questionnaire on this page and submit. Your submission is your acceptance of the terms below, the day it lands is your commencement date, and your booking is payable as set out in the terms. Nothing moves out of your account yet.

- We read every line before we speak to you, so the first call starts where it should, not at the beginning. We contact you within two working days to arrange access to your numbers.

- We connect your data and build the first version of your live dashboard, a standard build fed from your own database, typically up within a day or two of access being granted: your turnover, your departments, what is moving and what has stopped, on your own phone, without waiting for anyone to phone you with figures. The first 50% falls due at that live dashboard, and that payment is the booking of your audit. You pay nothing before you can see your own numbers working.

- The audit runs, two to three weeks from commencement. Findings reach you in pieces as they are proven, not in one book at the end, because three weeks is too short to find everything first and act afterwards. Whatever we find, you can act on in the same week. While the audit runs you have us in your corner: two calls a week, short written updates on the other days, questions answered, quick fixes handed over as they land. That handholding period is a deliverable of the audit itself, not a courtesy.

- The audit is presented: the findings, the plan and everything behind them, in one book. The remaining 50% is due on that date. If it is not paid immediately, it remains due and payable from that date. Everything is yours to keep whether we ever work together again or not.

- You choose the road, or no road at all. No lock-in past the audit.

Scope

## What the audit covers

**Your money:** where your sales go, your real gross profit and how cash moves through the month. **Your stock:** how much cash sits on your shelves, what sells and what is dead weight you pay to hold. **Your ledger:** whether the figures your system shows you deserve trust. **Your ordering:** buying to demand or buying to habit, and what the gap costs weekly. **Your leaks:** shrinkage, waste, pricing errors and margin lost at the till. Everything tested against your own till and ledger data, nothing quoted to you until it has passed that test.

The deliverables

## What you get, and keep

### 1. The live dashboard

A standard build fed from your own database, up within the first days and running right through the audit. It is a window on your business and our progress report to you in one place: you watch the store and you watch us working. It stays up after the audit, indefinitely, as long as the installations on your server that feed it are left undisturbed.

### 2. The handholding period

Direct access to us for the duration: two calls a week, one to report what has been found and one to ask what only you can answer, with short written updates in between. Interim findings and quick fixes handed over the week they are proven.

### 3. The findings

What is happening in your store, each finding stated in rand, with the arithmetic shown and the source named. A short read for your phone, the full findings for your desk and the working papers behind every figure.

[See a sample finding →](https://www.socialbrand.africa/audit/sample-findings/)

### 4. The plan

What to do, in what order, ranked by what each move puts back in your pocket, with owners and dates against every action.

### 5. The book

The whole audit compiled into one document at the end: findings, plan, systems notes, the record of what was found and what was already acted on. It closes the audit, it is not the first time you see any of it.

All five are yours to keep, use and act on, whether or not you ever work with us again.

Scope of advice

## The lane. What we advise on, and what we do not

The mandate is one thing: turn the business around. Every recommendation is measured against that and nothing else.

We advise on where money goes into the business. Which stock to buy first, which lines to carry, which suppliers to protect, where margin leaks, what the range should be. The bias is stated openly: toward the trading business, toward turnover and toward margin. Paying the supplier who keeps your shelves full is a buying decision, so trade creditors sit inside the lane.

Your debt sits outside the lane and stays outside. We are not financiers, bankers or financial advisors. We will not tell you how to restructure a loan, who to settle with or how to raise money. What we will do is show you what the trading business can carry, honestly and in your own numbers, so you and the people qualified for those decisions can make them on real information. Also outside: tax, statutory accounting, labour law and legal opinion. For those, use a registered professional, and we gladly work alongside yours.

Consent

## Permission. Nothing happens without yours

Nothing is done with your data or inside your business without your express permission first. That covers what we may copy from your system and what we may do with it, any new use of your data beyond what was agreed, any instruction reaching your staff (we advise you, you mandate them, we do not issue instructions in your business), any approach to a supplier, landlord, bank or other third party on your behalf, and any use of your business name anywhere. You may withdraw any permission at any time.

Two permissions make the audit work. Your submission of this page grants the first: permission to read and analyse the business data you share with us, read-only, for this audit. The second is a separate short authorisation letter, signed when we connect your dashboard: it lets us collect, each night, the backup copy your system already writes on its own. Nothing is installed on your machine, nothing changes on it and nothing is ever written back to your system. Not a price, not a stock figure, not a correction. Your database is read, never touched, and your tills are never slowed because collection happens hours after they stop.

What we need

## What we need from you and your team

The audit fails without these, said plainly so there is no surprise later.

- **Your people take it seriously.** This is the one that decides whether any of it works. An action plan nobody implements returns nothing, and it will still have cost you the fee. Your manager and your buyers need to hear from you, not from us, that this is not optional.

- **You back it publicly.** If the floor believes you are only half behind it, they will wait it out. Half a mandate is worse than none.

- **Somebody answers within a working day.** Usually you or your manager. Name that person on the form.

- **Documents arrive when asked for.** Management accounts, supplier statements, a recent stock take, till reports, whatever exists. Photos of printed pages are fine. If something does not exist, say so. A missing report is a finding, not a failure.

- **The authorisations above, when we ask for them.**

- **Honest answers, including uncomfortable ones.** We will find what is there. Being told first is always cheaper.

Timing

## The clock, in plain terms

Your commencement date is the day your submission lands, and the two to three week count to your delivered audit runs from that day. Delays on access, paperwork or answers do not pause the clock, they eat into it. The same goes for what we hand you during the handholding period: what you implement immediately starts paying immediately, what waits costs you. Move fast and the audit starts paying for itself before it is even delivered.

If a payment that has fallen due is withheld, the handholding stops until the account is right, and the clock keeps counting. It is your audit and your weeks, spend them well. If the timing of a payment is difficult, say so and we stagger it. That is a conversation, not a concession, and better had before than after.

How findings move

## The audit changes as we learn, the deal does not

We do not yet know everything about your business, and neither do you. That is the point of the work. Each finding changes what is worth doing next: a week on availability may show the real problem is buying. When that happens we say so and agree the new direction with you before following it. What never changes is the fee, the mandate and the lane. What changes is where the effort points.

On projections

## What a number is worth

Numbers about the past are measurements from your own system, reconciled against your own reports, and we stand behind them. Numbers about the future are best estimates on the facts of the day, never a promise or a guarantee. Context moves: a competitor opens, a supplier stops, weather kills a weekend. So every projection comes with its assumptions written next to it, and when an assumption breaks we tell you the number changed rather than let you plan against it.

Read this before you submit

## The terms

- **Service:** Store Health Audit, one store, fixed fee R35,000. Fixed means fixed, it does not move with the hours. No VAT is charged at present.

- **Ordering:** the audit is ordered by submitting this page, or by a verbal go-ahead, or by written email confirmation. Any of the three brings these terms into force, and the date of that order is the commencement date. Where the order is verbal or by email, this page is sent to you as the record of the terms.

- **Payment:** the audit is payable on ordering, in two halves. The first R17,500 falls due when the first version of your live dashboard is up, built from your own data, typically a day or two after access is granted. That payment is the booking of your audit. The remaining R17,500 falls due on the date the audit is ready and presented. If it is not paid immediately, it remains due and payable from that date.

- **Timeline:** two to three weeks from the commencement date.

- **Handholding:** consultant access, interim findings and quick fixes for the duration are a deliverable of the audit. Withheld due payment suspends this deliverable until settled. The timeline does not pause.

- **The Virtual Retail Direction option:** the Store Health Audit is a prerequisite of Virtual Retail Direction, direction is only sold on the back of a completed or running audit. Within 30 days of commencement you may indicate, agree or order Virtual Retail Direction (R25,000 a month). The audit’s second R17,500 is then reallocated to your first month of direction, which is the second month of the relationship. If you have already paid it, your first direction month reads as R17,500 paid upfront and the remaining R7,500 is due on the first of that month. If you have not yet paid it, it stands as a discount on the audit and the full R25,000 for the first direction month is due on the first of that month. Either way the total is the same: the audit plus your first month of direction comes to R42,500. If you stop at the audit, the balance is simply the balance and nothing else happens.

- **The dashboard stays, indefinitely.** The initial dashboard is a generic build, fed from your database. Whatever you decide after the audit, it stays up indefinitely at no further charge, on one condition: the installations on your server that feed it are not disrupted or deleted. No maintenance is guaranteed. If the feed breaks, the machine changes or the installations are removed, restoring it is new work by arrangement, not a standing obligation.

- **Your data stays yours.** Never sold, never shared, never shown to another retailer, never used to benchmark you to anyone by name. Want it deleted, it is deleted. Want it handed over, it is handed over.

- **Confidentiality runs both ways.** Neither side discusses the other’s business, terms or findings with anyone outside it without written permission. Naming you as a client anywhere requires your agreement first. A signed mutual confidentiality agreement is available on request, same day. Our methods and tools stay ours.

- **The work is recorded.** Every hour is logged on the day against what it produced. Ask for the log at any time and it is given without editing. The fee is fixed and the hours do not change it.

- **Advisory basis:** findings and rand figures are our best estimates from the data and access you provide, and depend on that data being accurate and complete. Where a gap limits us we say so plainly rather than guess.

- **No guaranteed result.** We do not guarantee a financial outcome. Results depend on execution, market conditions and factors outside anyone’s control.

- **Not professional advice:** Nothing in the audit is financial, legal, tax or accounting advice.

- **We never touch your money.** We do not access, move or change funds. We advise. You decide and you act.

- **Agreement:** your order, whether by submitting this page, by verbal go-ahead or by written email confirmation, is your acceptance of these terms and forms the working agreement between you and Social Brands Investments (Pty) Ltd, commencing on the date of that order. Keep the downloaded copy for your records.

What happens next

## After the audit: the road

Three options, and the plan works with all of them. You own it either way, that is deliberate, and it is why the audit is worth buying on its own. What the plan will not do is manage itself: a recovery plan in a folder returns nothing.

1

### Do it yourself

Take the plan, run it with your own team.

2

### Virtual Retail Direction

R25,000 a month, remote. The month-to-month work of pointing at the right thing, checking it happened and adjusting when the store or the town moves. Your database read every night with exception checks run before you are awake, weekly analytics, weekly direction calls with you and your managers, a monthly owner report in plain language. Your team executes, we direct. Month to month, billed on the first, thirty days notice either way, no lock-in. Recommended for three months, because a store does not turn in four weeks. Order it within 30 days of your audit’s commencement and the audit’s second R17,500 goes toward your first month, as set out in the terms above.

3

### Full operational management

R100,000 a month, twelve month minimum. We run the turnaround for you, on the floor, ordering discipline and systems work included. Virtual Retail Direction is included.

Optional add-ons to either road, priced on enquiry: the module apps (Bloom for ordering, Root for suppliers, Stem for finance, Rhythm for people, Mark for pricing, Vigil for live monitoring) and custom-built applications where a tool will pay for itself. The clearest example is a production costing engine, a bill of materials for your butchery, bakery and deli, scoped after the audit shows where it earns its keep.

Decide all of this after the audit, on the findings, not now. Nothing about the credit should push the decision.

Start here

## The questionnaire

This is the start of your audit, not admin. We read every line before we speak to you. About twenty minutes, no preparation needed. There are no wrong answers. Where you are not sure, give your best estimate or write “not sure”. Rough is fine. We would rather have your honest guess than a blank.

# A sample audit finding | SocialBrand

URL: https://www.socialbrand.africa/audit/sample-findings/

See the format of a Store Health Audit finding: the rand figure, the evidence and the action, illustrated on a fictional store with generated data.

[Home](https://www.socialbrand.africa/) / [Order the audit](https://www.socialbrand.africa/audit/) / Sample finding

See the format

# What an audit finding looks like

Four findings from a fictional store, shown in the same shape a real finding reaches you: the number, the evidence, the action. This is what R35,000 buys: not a slide deck of opinions, arithmetic you can check.

**Generated, illustrative example.** Fairview SuperMart and Fairview Liquor are the same fictional stores used in the [live demo](https://www.socialbrand.africa/demo/). They do not exist, and no figure below comes from a real store or a real client. Any resemblance to a real business is coincidental. Real clients’ findings are never published, named or shown to anyone outside their own business.

Ledger

### Phantom stock, 200g Rooibos Twin-Pack

R38,400

**Evidence:** 14 lines flagged store-wide, led by this one. Ledger shows 40 units on hand. Last recorded sale was 71 days ago, and the last physical count was never done. Under the Presence Law, a line with no recent sale and no recent count is a claim, not a fact.

**Action:** Physical count of the 14 flagged lines, week 1. Receiving code fixed at source so the twin-pack stops posting to the single-unit code. Owner: stock controller, by Friday.

Availability

### Stockouts on the top 20 lines

R61,000 / month

**Evidence:** True rate of sale, corrected for the days each line stood empty, shows six of the top 20 sellers running out an average of 4.2 days a month. At current margin, that is the estimated monthly sale lost while the shelf sat empty.

**Action:** Reorder points reset on the six lines to reflect true demand, not the days they were empty. Owner: buyer, live from week 2.

Margin

### Till price mismatches on promoted lines

R14,200 / month

**Evidence:** Nine promoted lines checked against the till file. Three were still charging the pre-promotion price at the till, two had expired promotions still active. Estimate built from actual sales volume at the wrong price, not a sample.

**Action:** Weekly promotion-to-till reconciliation added to the Friday routine. Owner: front-end supervisor, starting immediately.

Buying

### Capital tied in slow stock, ordered on habit

R22,000 tied up

**Evidence:** Eleven lines ordered on a fixed weekly quantity regardless of what actually sold. Demonstrated demand supports less than half the ordered volume on eight of them. The rest is capital sitting on a shelf, not working.

**Action:** Order quantities on the eleven lines cut to demonstrated demand, phased over two cycles so the shelf never looks empty. Owner: buyer, from week 2.

A real audit runs to considerably more findings than four, across money, stock, ledger, ordering and leaks, each backed by its own working papers. This is the format, not the length.

## See the platform behind it

These findings come from the same kind of live, generated data as the interactive demo. Explore the fuller breakdown on Fairview’s own numbers.

[Open the live demo](https://www.socialbrand.africa/demo/)[Order your own audit](https://www.socialbrand.africa/audit/#questionnaire)
